method: Independent semantic-plausibility adjudication of a 60-edge deterministic sample from out/graph.json. This is NOT ground truth and NOT an accuracy measurement -- it does not re-check the resolver's decision-number/date match (which is the resolver's own job); it asks only whether the target GR's subject matter is a plausible thing for the citing GR to be citing, given the citing GR's own subject and the ~600-1000 characters of Marathi text around the evidence sentence.
caveats: This checks semantic coherence of SUBJECTS, not factual correctness of the resolution -- a wrong-but-topically-similar target (e.g. the wrong year's instance of the same recurring scheme) would still be scored PLAUSIBLE by this method. It cannot catch that class of error, which is precisely the kind of error the resolver's number+date matching is supposed to prevent, so this check is complementary, not a substitute.

'subject' fields come from crawled portal metadata (English), not from the Marathi record itself; a wrong or mistranslated portal subject could make a correct resolution look implausible or vice versa.

Marathi comprehension for the ~15 edges I read in full source context was done by me directly (no model call); I am not a certified Marathi speaker and could misread the administrative jargon or file-number series conventions.

For several edges (mostly School Education -> Finance appropriation/fund-distribution citations) the target subject line is generic ('Fund Distribution', 'Fund Release 2025-26'); I judged these PLAUSIBLE on the strength of the well-documented natural-dependency pattern (a department's appropriation release citing Finance's own fund-distribution circular) rather than on independently confirmed subject content, and marked them lower-confidence and flagged for human review.

Sample is 60 of 4,815 edges (~1.2%); with zero IMPLAUSIBLE found in this sample, a 95%-ish upper bound on the true implausibility rate is still meaningfully above zero -- absence of evidence in 60 edges is not evidence of a zero error rate across the graph.

I did not re-verify the underlying decision-number digit-signature matching, the +-3-day window logic, or check for the same-number/same-date collision failure modes described in CLAUDE.md -- those are the resolver's job and explicitly out of scope for this adjudication per the task instructions.

No model (Groq) calls were needed or used; all 60 verdicts were reached by reading English subject metadata plus, for ~15 edges where the subject alone was ambiguous or too generic, the Marathi source text directly. This means there is no independent second reader (human or model) confirming my own Marathi reading of those ~15 edges.

sample.selection: Loaded out/graph.json edges as a list (list index == edge_index, already in file order). Built enumerate(edges) pairs, sorted by index (a no-op since already ordered), then called random.seed(42); random.sample(indexed_list, 60) to draw 60 (index, edge) pairs without replacement. Final verdict list is re-sorted by edge_index for readability.
